prompt:
You are a careful equity research analyst. Assess the competitive advantages (economic moat) and pricing power of the publicly listed company "Johnson Controls International plc" (ticker JCI), and list its competitors. Use the most recent information you know. Never invent figures: use null when unsure. Be specific (products, numbers, years).

Reply with ONLY one JSON object, no other text, in exactly this shape:
{
 "name": "official company name", "ticker": "JCI", "industry": "industry in a few words",
 "markets": ["the main product markets it competes in"],
 "mission": {"statement": "the company's own official mission statement, word for word as it publishes it; null if you are not sure of the exact wording (never paraphrase here)",
             "source": "where it is published, e.g. company website or 2025 annual report, or null",
             "plain": "what the mission means, in one short simple sentence"},
 "about": {"plain": "3-4 short sentences explaining what the company does, in simple everyday words a 12-year-old would understand; no jargon",
           "customers": "who buys from it, in one simple sentence",
           "everyday": "one sentence linking it to something ordinary people know or use, or null",
           "money": [ {"part": "business line in simple words", "share": decimal share of sales or null, "plain": "what it sells there, in a few simple words", "tag": "main|new|moonshot"} ]  (its main ways of making money, largest first, up to 6; also include any new business line or one with explosive, moonshot potential even if its sales are still small. tag: "main" = an established line that brings in a large part of sales; "new" = launched or entered in roughly the last 3 years; "moonshot" = could grow many times over or reshape the company, e.g. a new technology or market, even if unproven. Give each line one tag, the one that fits best)},
 "summary": "2-3 plain-English sentences on whether and why it has a competitive advantage",
 "pricingPower": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "specific evidence, e.g. price rises and what happened to volumes"},
 "moats": [ {"source": one of ["Brand and intangible assets","Switching costs","Network effects","Cost advantage and scale","Efficient scale","Counter-positioning","Process power (hard-to-copy know-how)","Cornered resource (exclusive asset or talent)"], "strength": "strong|moderate|weak|none", "evidence": "one or two specific sentences"} ]  (all 8 sources, in that order),
 "customers": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "customer satisfaction and loyalty: retention, NPS, reviews, repeat purchase"},
 "talent": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "ability to attract and keep top talent: employer rankings, reputation, pay"},
 "product": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "is the product best in class? independent benchmarks, awards, ecosystem"},
 "competitors": [ {"name": "company name", "ticker": "main listing ticker (exchange suffix if not US, e.g. 005930.KS) or null if private",
                   "usTicker": "ticker of its US listing or ADR that files reports with the SEC, or null", "overlap": "high|medium|low",
                   "note": "where they compete"} ]  (every significant competitor, most direct first, up to 15; include major private ones with ticker null),
 "estimates": [ {"name": "company name", "fy": "FY2025", "currency": "USD", "revenueUSDm": number, "revenueGrowth3y": decimal, "grossMargin": decimal, "operatingMargin": decimal, "netMargin": decimal} ]
   (approximate latest fiscal-year figures for the company itself and for every listed competitor; decimals, e.g. 0.42; null if unknown),
 "marketShare": [ {"market": "market name", "measure": "revenue|units|shipments|...", "latestYear": "2025", "earlierYear": "2020",
                   "rows": [ {"name": "company name", "latest": decimal or null, "earlier": decimal or null} ] } ]  (up to 3 of its main markets, the company and its main rivals),
 "threats": ["specific things that could weaken its advantage"],
 "ceo": {"name": "current CEO", "founder": true or false, "since": "YYYY", "background": "e.g. electrical engineer, Stanford MBA"},
 "checklist": { "<id>": {"verdict": "yes|partly|no|unknown", "evidence": "one specific sentence with names, numbers or examples"} }  for EVERY id below:
   "c1": Rule Breaker #1: is it the leader of an important industry that is still emerging and growing fast?
   "c2": Rule Breaker #2: why do customers choose it over rivals (brand, better value, innovation, culture, leadership), and is that advantage hard to copy and likely to last many years?
   "c3": Rule Breaker #5: do ordinary people recognise the name, is it the default leader in its field (like Google, Amazon, NVIDIA, Tesla, Intuitive Surgical, Netflix), and would customers recommend its product?
   "c4": Does it have an inspiring mission it keeps emphasising, with management driven by purpose rather than money? If it spends 10 years doing this, would it matter?
   "c6": What is the general public consensus about the company and its products or services? When people hear the name, what are the first few descriptive words that come to mind? Start the evidence with those words in quotes (e.g. “innovative, premium, reliable”), then say whether that impression is mostly positive.
   "c7": Is its total addressable market large and growing, riding a secular trend (like CRWD, NVDA, TSLA, AMZN)?
   "c8": Does it have room to expand into big new markets: in its name, its technology or its vision?
   "m1": Is the CEO a visionary with a clear picture of the future?
   "m2": Is the CEO a founder (or acting like one): long-term thinking, working extraordinarily hard, pouring heart and soul into building something that outlives them?
   "m4": Does the CEO lead by serving employees and customers?
   "m5": Has the CEO deliberately built a strong, distinctive culture that keeps inventing new products and technologies?
   "m6": Is the CEO deeply hands-on with the product and technology, ideally with an engineering background?
   "m7": Is the CEO a person of great character who cares about something bigger than profit? For successor CEOs: is stewardship aimed at the benefit of humanity?
   "m7b": Has the CEO been invited to give a commencement speech at a top university (Stanford, Harvard, MIT, etc.)? Name it.
   "m8b": Does the CEO have a distinctive, memorable personality (like Elon Musk, Alex Karp, Larry Page)?
   "m9": Has the CEO a strong record of execution and results?
   "m10": Is the CEO and company known for frugality (like Bezos's door desk)?
   "c10": Do its products solve problems for people all over the world, greatly improving the lives of a very large number of people (like NFLX, GOOG, ISRG)?
   "p2": Is what it builds extremely hard to do, and important to the world?
   "f1": Has revenue grown in almost every one of the last five years?
   "f2": Have gross and operating margins risen over the last five years?
   "f3": Is debt low compared with cash and cash flow, with positive shareholders' equity?
   "f4": Have operating income and operating cash flow risen over the last five years?
   "v1": Is its main product clearly the best in its field, with a practical reason an ordinary person can understand for choosing it over every alternative (like NVIDIA over AMD)?
   "v2": Is it widely seen as one of the best companies to work for (culture, mission, reputation, employer rankings)? Cite rankings.
   "c5": Do its products make the world better? If it disappeared overnight, who would notice and miss it, and why?
 "asOf": "YYYY-MM of the newest information you used"
}

result.name: Johnson Controls International plc
result.industry: Commercial HVAC, building controls and fire and security systems
markets: Commercial HVAC equipment (York chillers, air handlers, rooftop units, heat pumps)
Data-center thermal management (chillers, Silent-Aire air handling, coolant distribution units)
Building automation and controls (Metasys, OpenBlue digital platform)
Fire detection and suppression (Simplex, Grinnell, Tyco, Zettler)

mission.statement: Our vision is a safe, comfortable and sustainable world.
mission.source: Johnson Controls FY2025 annual report to shareholders (published as the company's vision; no separate mission statement was found)
mission.plain: Johnson Controls wants the buildings people live and work in to be safe, comfortable and kind to the planet.

about.plain: Johnson Controls makes the big machines that heat and cool large buildings, like hospitals, airports, factories and the giant data centers that run AI. It also makes the systems that control a building's temperature, fire alarms, sprinklers and security cameras. After it sells the equipment, it earns steady money servicing and fixing it for years. It sold its home air-conditioning business in 2025 to focus on big commercial buildings.
about.customers: Owners and operators of large buildings such as data centers, hospitals, universities, offices, factories and governments.
about.everyday: The fire alarm, sprinklers or air conditioning in your school, hospital or office may well be made or serviced by Johnson Controls (brands like York, Simplex and Tyco).

money.plain: chillers, air handlers, controls, fire and security systems
maintenance, repairs, retrofits and monitoring of building systems
chillers and air systems for AI and cloud data centers; expected to be a high-teens percent of FY2026 sales
units that pipe liquid coolant to AI chips; pipeline above $1 billion, first shipments in late FY2026
software and AI that runs buildings more efficiently

result.summary: Johnson Controls has a moderate competitive advantage built on a huge installed base of chillers, controls and fire systems that generates recurring service revenue, long-standing brands (York, Metasys, Simplex, Tyco) and a global service network. It competes head-to-head with Trane, Carrier, Daikin, Siemens and Honeywell, so it is not dominant, but strong data-center cooling demand (orders up 27% organically and backlog of $21.0B in Q3 FY2026) and a new Danaher-style business system are strengthening its position.

pricingPower.evidence: Gross margin rose from 34.4% in FY2022 to 36.4% in FY2025 on a continuing-operations basis even as sales grew, and in Q3 FY2026 sales rose 9% with segment margins up 110-260 basis points, but commercial HVAC bids are competitive against Trane, Carrier and Daikin.

moats.evidence: York chillers, Metasys controls and Simplex/Tyco fire brands are trusted by engineers and specifiers, and JCI has been on Ethisphere's World's Most Ethical Companies list 18 times, but brand matters less than specs and price in bids.
Once a Metasys building-automation system or fire-alarm network is installed, replacing it is costly and disruptive, which keeps customers buying JCI service (services were 31.7% of FY2025 sales).
The OpenBlue platform gathers data across many buildings, but there is little evidence that more users make the product meaningfully better for each customer.
With $23.6B of FY2025 sales and about 90,000 employees, JCI has one of the largest direct service networks in buildings, though Trane, Carrier and Daikin have similar scale.
Large-chiller and fire-system markets have a handful of global suppliers, but none is protected from competition.
Its business model of equipment plus service is the same as Trane's and Carrier's.

Decades of York chiller engineering and a new proprietary 80/20 and Lean business system, which cut one product's time to market by 40% and more than quadrupled capacity on an air-handler line, are hard to copy quickly.
It has no exclusive assets; its record $21.0B backlog secures future work but is not a cornered resource.

customers.evidence: Orders rose 27% organically and backlog 32% to $21.0B in Q3 FY2026, showing strong demand from data centers, hospitals and universities, and the installed base drives repeat service work, but public satisfaction data (NPS) is not disclosed.

talent.evidence: JCI has made Ethisphere's World's Most Ethical Companies list 18 times and was on Fortune's 2025 Change the World list for data-center cooling, but it does not appear near the top of mainstream best-employer rankings such as Fortune's 100 Best Companies to Work For.

product.evidence: York chillers and Silent-Aire air handlers are leading choices for data-center cooling and won Fortune's 2025 Change the World recognition, but Trane, Carrier, Daikin and Vertiv offer comparable products and Trane is often seen as the technology leader in commercial HVAC.

competitors.name: Trane Technologies
competitors.note: Largest U.S. commercial HVAC rival in chillers, data-center cooling, controls and service.

competitors.name: Siemens AG (Smart Infrastructure)
competitors.note: Building automation, fire safety and security systems competing with Metasys, Simplex and Tyco.

competitors.name: Honeywell International
competitors.note: Building automation, fire alarms (Notifier) and security products.

competitors.name: Schneider Electric
competitors.note: Building management software (EcoStruxure) and data-center cooling through Motivair and Uniflair.

competitors.note: Fire protection and security installation and service in North America and Europe.

threats: A slowdown or pause in AI data-center construction, which the CFO expects to be a high-teens percent of FY2026 revenue and possibly one-third within 3-5 years.
Direct-to-chip liquid cooling could reduce the need for large chillers and air handlers, favoring rivals such as Vertiv and Schneider if JCI's new coolant distribution units lag.
Intense competition from Trane, Carrier, Daikin and low-cost Chinese makers (Midea, Gree) in chillers and applied HVAC.
Ongoing litigation over AFFF firefighting foams made by its former Tyco Fire Products unit.
Weak EMEA growth (1% organic in Q3 FY2026) tied to Middle East conflicts, and exposure to commercial construction cycles.
Execution risk as a new CEO rolls out a Danaher-style business system and continues portfolio divestitures.
Cyberattacks on connected building systems (JCI itself suffered a major ransomware attack in 2023).

ceo.name: Joakim Weidemanis
ceo.background: Swedish industrial executive; 13 years at Danaher (Executive Vice President 2017-2024 overseeing Diagnostics and China, earlier leading Product ID and Water Quality), and before that executive roles at Mettler Toledo and ABB

c1.evidence: JCI is a top-tier player in commercial HVAC and building systems, a mature industry, but it is a leader in the fast-growing niche of AI data-center cooling, where orders drove Americas orders up 37% in Q3 FY2026.

c2.evidence: Customers choose JCI for its installed base, York chiller engineering and global service network, which are hard to copy, but Trane, Carrier and Daikin offer similar strengths, so the edge is not unique.

c3.evidence: Ordinary people rarely recognize Johnson Controls or York by name, and Trane and Carrier are better-known HVAC brands.

c4.evidence: Its vision 'a safe, comfortable and sustainable world' and decarbonization message are emphasized, but management communication centers on organic growth, margins and an adjusted EPS target of about $5.05 for FY2026.

c6.evidence: “industrial, HVAC, old-line, building systems” come to mind for those who know it; the impression is neutral to mildly positive, though many people do not know the name at all.

c7.evidence: Building HVAC and controls is a very large market riding secular trends in AI data centers, electrification and decarbonization, reflected in a record $21.0B backlog, up 32% organically in Q3 FY2026.

c8.evidence: It is expanding into liquid cooling (CDU pipeline above $1 billion), modular data centers through its investment in Armada, and AI-driven building software (OpenBlue), but remains a building-systems company.

m1.evidence: Weidemanis has set a clear picture of JCI as a focused thermal-management and mission-critical building-systems company run on a proprietary 80/20 and Lean business system, but it is an operational rather than visionary agenda.

m2.evidence: He is a hired CEO (since March 2025) who emphasizes long-term operating discipline and 'Going to Gemba' factory visits, but he is not a founder.

m4.evidence: His Lean business system puts the customer and front-line teams at the center (e.g., cutting lead times and time to market by 40% on one product), but there is little public evidence of a servant-leadership style.

m5.evidence: He is deliberately building a Danaher-style continuous-improvement culture, which so far has produced faster product launches and capacity gains rather than a stream of new technologies.

m6.evidence: Weidemanis is hands-on with operations and factory floors through the business system, but no engineering degree is disclosed in company materials.

m7.evidence: No controversies are known, and the company stresses ethics (18 times on Ethisphere's list), but there is too little public record to judge his character beyond professional conduct.

m7b.evidence: No commencement speech by Joakim Weidemanis at a top university was found.

m8b.evidence: Weidemanis is a low-profile operator with a conventional corporate public persona.

m9.evidence: Since he took over in March 2025, JCI raised FY2026 guidance to about 8% organic growth and adjusted EPS of about $5.05, Q3 FY2026 adjusted EPS rose 35% to $1.42, and earlier at Danaher he ran large Diagnostics and China businesses.

m10.evidence: The 80/20 business system focuses resources and cut capital spending to $243M in the first nine months of FY2026 from $304M a year earlier, but JCI is not known for a frugal culture.

c10.evidence: Its fire, security and HVAC systems protect and cool hospitals, schools and data centers around the world, but the benefit is indirect and rivals supply the same products.

p2.evidence: Designing large chillers and life-safety systems for mission-critical buildings is demanding and important, but several global competitors can do it too.

f1.evidence: Continuing-operations sales rose every year from $20,637M (FY2022) to $22,331M (FY2023), $22,952M (FY2024) and $23,596M (FY2025), and reported sales also grew from FY2020 ($22,317M) to FY2021 ($23,668M).

f2.evidence: Gross margin on continuing operations rose every year from 34.4% (FY2022) to 36.4% (FY2025), but operating margin has been held back by restructuring and impairment charges of $546M in FY2025 and $1,049M in FY2023.

f3.evidence: Debt of $9,475M versus $641M of cash at June 30, 2026 is high relative to cash, but it is about 1.9 times net debt to EBITDA, equity is positive at $13,515M, and nine-month operating cash flow was $2,572M.

f4.evidence: Continuing-operations operating cash flow went from $1,856M (FY2023) to $1,568M (FY2024) to $2,554M (FY2025), and net income attributable fell from $1,849M (FY2023) to $1,705M (FY2024), so the rise has not been steady.

v1.evidence: York chillers and Metasys controls are strong, but there is no clear, practical reason a buyer would pick JCI over Trane, Carrier or Daikin in every case.

v2.evidence: JCI is recognized for ethics (Ethisphere's World's Most Ethical Companies 18 times) and was on Fortune's 2025 Change the World list, but it does not rank on Fortune's 100 Best Companies to Work For.

c5.evidence: Building owners, hospitals and data-center operators who rely on its service technicians and installed systems would be disrupted, but Trane, Carrier, Siemens and Honeywell could largely fill the gap.
